podcast.title: Band Formation at McMaster University (2004)
podcast.body: The band's core began forming on the first and second days Max Kermann attended McMaster University in Hamilton in 2004. Max, who was primarily interested in finding bandmates, met Mike DeAngeles on day one by asking about his favorite bands (The Weakerthans) and if he played guitar. On day two, Nick Dica introduced himself to Max because Max was wearing a Sam Roberts Band T-shirt, and upon learning Nick played bass, he was also invited to join. "You're literally the first and second day that you were in university."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Arkells - In Their Own Words: Part 1

podcast.title: Initial Band Name: Charlemagne (2004-2007/2008)
podcast.body: The band initially performed under the name Charlemagne from their first gig at the McMaster Battle of the Bands until late 2007 or early 2008. They were forced to change their name after another band named Charlemagne on MySpace threatened to sue them. "We call ourselves Charlemagne as our first band name."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Arkells - In Their Own Words: Part 1

podcast.title: Name Change to Arkells (Late 2007/Early 2008)
podcast.body: The name change from Charlemagne to Arkells occurred under extreme pressure when Dino Lone Records needed a new name in 45 minutes for an EP flyer to be inserted into the City and Colour record. Max Kermann and Mike DeAngeles, who lived on Arkell Street at the time, proposed the name in a last-minute effort, noting its 60s Motown-esque sound. "So then we frantically got on the phone. I was at the library and McMaster, I still remember. And we called everyone, we got to change the name now because we've been sitting on this kind of decision for a long time and we just hadn't got around to it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Arkells - In Their Own Words: Part 1

podcast.title: MySpace Contact from Producer Tony Hoffer (2013)
podcast.body: Despite previous unsuccessful attempts to contact producer Tony Hoffer through his manager, Hoffer personally reached out to Arkells via MySpace in 2013. He had discovered them after watching a live session of theirs, thinking they were a "cool band" and asking if they were "thinking of recording anytime soon." "he reached out to us on MySpace. On MySpace saying like, hey, you guys are, wait, in 2013, he reaches out on MySpace."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Arkells - In Their Own Words:  Part 2

podcast.title: Pyeongchang 2018 Winter Olympics "Scam Trip"
podcast.body: The band "drifted" into performing at the Canada House during the 2018 Pyeongchang Winter Olympics. The opportunity arose after they jokingly tweeted to Art Canada and Canada House (who were using "Knockin' at the Door" as a theme song) about covering their expenses for a trip. Within three days, they were on a plane, flying coach for a 14.5-hour flight without bringing instruments due to last-minute arrangements. They played three house-party style shows over the last five days of the Olympics, largely for athletes who were "ready to party" having finished their events, playing on the ground because the stage was only big enough for drums. "Yeah, that's a 14 and a half hour flight. Yeah. Did they, at least spring for premium economy? No, we were absolutely not. We were in coach."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Arkells - In Their Own Words:  Part 2

podcast.title: Adoption of Hamilton as Home City
podcast.body: Although the members are originally from different parts of Ontario (Newmarket, London, Mississauga, Guelph, and Toronto), the band adopted Hamilton as its official home. This is because the band was "born" there, all its formative experiences, first sold-out shows, and connections to the music scene happened in Hamilton, making it their true musical home. "But as a band all our formative experiences happened in Hamilton, you know, like we're never going to know the clubs in any other city the way we know the clubs in Hamilton or you know, our connections to the music scene and all those really important things for us happened in Hamilton, you know."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Arkells - In Their Own Words: Part 1

podcast.title: Anthony's Baby Born Before Morton's Field Show
podcast.body: Anthony's baby was born approximately 36 to 48 hours before the band's "The Rally" show at Morton's Field. His wife was due June 10th, and the show fell within a two-week window. Anthony did soundcheck the day before after his baby was born at 8 AM, then slept upright in a hospital chair, and drove his wife and newborn home the morning of the show, performing on "fumes." "My wife was due June 10th. And this was like the one show that was slotted in kind of like a two week before, two week after a period."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Canadian Band Prolificacy
podcast.body: The Arkells are highlighted as one of the most prolific Canadian bands of the past decade, consistently writing, recording, and releasing new material. "Arkels have been one of the most prolific Canadian bands of the last decade."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 2020 Xmas Show

podcast.title: Collaborative Songwriting Process
podcast.body: While Max Kermann typically initiates the songs and is the chief lyricist, the songwriting process is highly collaborative. The other band members provide significant input through editing and questioning, ensuring clarity and improving the lyrics. All members share in the songwriting split, reflecting an "all for one, one for all" approach. "Yeah, I mean, I start the songs, but the more we do it, the more there's a pretty good heavy dose of editing going on from the guys where I go, is there a better way to say this? Or is this part clear? So it is very collaborative in that sense."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Arkells - In Their Own Words: Part 1

podcast.title: Continuous Audience Engagement
podcast.body: The band prioritizes consistent engagement with their listeners, understanding the importance of continuously supplying new songs, shows, and special online content. They believe that for most bands, showing earnest care and being visible is crucial, as audiences expect to be engaged constantly. "working consistently and being loyal to your listeners and, and providing them with, you know, the service of new songs and shows and all those things, I think, uh, is really important to remember that."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Arkells - In Their Own Words:  Part 2

podcast.title: Continuous Evolution of Songs Post-Release
podcast.body: The band acknowledges that they have no control over how songs evolve in people's lives after release. They find it interesting to see where their music lands, citing examples like "Knockin' at the Door" being used at the Olympics and "11-11" at weddings, appreciating that songs "can land in interesting places." "You put someone in the world and you go, oh, like knock at the door, I ended up being played at the Olympics. And like 11-11 was played at people's weddings. You know, it's funny how, you know, you have no control over that, but they can land in interesting places."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Arkells - In Their Own Words:  Part 2

podcast.title: Embrace of "Hollow Notes" Sound
podcast.body: During the production of "Michigan Left," the band underwent a "turning point" where they became open to more influences, particularly synth sounds referred to as "Hollow notes." Previously, they "hated Hollow notes" and focused on a guitar-driven, edgy sound for "Jackson Square," but on "Michigan Left," they found these nuanced synth sounds "actually kind of sound interesting," leading to a slightly more nuanced record. "I hated Hollow notes before we made Michigan left. And then I was sort of, those synths actually kind of sound interesting."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Arkells - In Their Own Words:  Part 2

podcast.title: Extensive Touring and Performances
podcast.body: The band has a reputation for playing a vast number of shows, appearing "anywhere and everywhere" asked by their label or radio stations, including pop-up gigs and spontaneous busking. They estimate they've played hundreds of shows per year for over a decade, working between 175 and 200 days annually on musically directed activities. This volume of performance is suggested to have potentially surpassed the Ramones' lifetime total of 2250 shows. "We do say we do like a hundred a year for, we've been doing this for 12 years. 1200 shows."

podcast.title: Free Olympics Trip via Tweet
podcast.body: The band leveraged their public profile and a "statue" (likely a metaphorical reference to their influence or popularity) to secure free airline tickets to the Olympics simply by sending a tweet. "They have a statue that allowed them to blag free airline tickets to the Olympics after doing nothing more than a quick tweet."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Arkells - In Their Own Words: Part 1

podcast.title: Morton's Field "The Rally" Stadium Show
podcast.body: In 2017, the band curated a massive show at Morton's Field in Hamilton for 24,000 people, aiming to surpass their previous large shows. Collaborating with the Tiger-Cats, they designed the event from the ground up, as the facility hadn't hosted many concerts in decades since a Pink Floyd issue in the 70s. The event featured a curated bill, custom poster, a bike ride from downtown to the stadium, an artist flea market, and local businesses creating Arkells-themed products like beer, sausages, and cupcakes. A portion of proceeds went to Refuge, a healthcare organization for new Canadians, making it a "real communal event." "We got to curate the bill. We got to design the poster. We got to, we organized a bike ride along the Canis Street bike lanes from downtown to the stadium. We had an artist flea market beforehand."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Arkells - In Their Own Words:  Part 2

podcast.title: Pub Crawl Tradition
podcast.body: The band has a tradition when they return home for Christmas after a tour, where they gather with friends at a pub, throw credit cards into a hat, and draw them to determine who pays the tab. The last two people drawn pay, and the process repeats at the next pub, excluding those who already paid, until everyone has contributed. "The song is based on how the band catches up with friends when they come home for Christmas after a long tour."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Scarlet Fever during Michigan Left Recording
podcast.body: One of the band members contracted scarlet fever during the recording sessions for "Michigan Left" at The Bathhouse studio, requiring them to be quarantined and out of commission for a couple of days. "I got scarlet fever actually during that, uh, okay. During that recording session. You had to be quarantined."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Stadium-Filling Status
podcast.body: Arkells has achieved significant popularity, capable of filling stadiums for their performances. "Not only can they fill a stadium, more on that in a bit, they have a statue that allowed them to blag free airline tickets to the Olympics after doing nothing more than a quick tweet."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Arkells - In Their Own Words: Part 1

podcast.title: Value of a Professional Producer
podcast.body: After self-producing "Michigan Left," the band learned that hiring a professional producer is "actually a very helpful thing." They found it challenging as "kids doing something for the first time" to work through all the questions and decisions involved in making a record. They view a producer as a "part psychologist," "social worker," and "translator" who can communicate effectively with each musician, ensuring good vibes and progress. "hiring a producer is actually a very helpful thing because I do remember it being tough as a bunch of like kids doing something for the first time."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Arkells - In Their Own Words:  Part 2

podcast.title: Wedding Song Popularity
podcast.body: Several acoustic versions of Arkells' songs, including "1111," "My Heart's All Yours," and "And Then Some," have become popular choices for first dances at weddings. The band regularly receives emails and videos from couples using their music for these special occasions, considering it a "very cool" and precious recognition. "Like that 1111 acoustic version has been used at like first dances for weddings, like countless times. Same thing with our acoustic versions of my heart, so it's yours. And, and then some, those three songs like we get in the summertime, like a couple of emails every week with videos from someone's wedding."

xref.title: Meeting Tim Oxford and Joining Arkells (2012)
xref.body: Anthony met Tim Oxford while playing bass in a cover band. Tim later called Anthony during the middle of his Warped Tour with Il Scarlett in 2012, inviting him to join Arkells as their keyboardist, as their previous one was returning to school. Anthony learned the material on the road and joined them two days after returning from tour. "So Tim calls me in the middle of that tour and goes, you know, our keyboardist is going back to school and we need someone to come in."

xref.title: Education and Entry into Arkells
xref.body: Dan Griffith attended McMaster University with Max Kermann, Mike DeAngeles, and Nick Dica. He joined Arkells a little after the initial trio started jamming, becoming their keyboard player until he left to go back to school. "So Dan went to Mac with us. Okay. And he joined the band a little after the three of us started jamming and with our original drummer."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Entry into Arkells and Professionalism
xref.body: Tim Oxford joined Arkells after attending audio school and networking through various pub gigs. He was introduced to the band by their previous keyboard player who mentioned they needed a drummer. His professionalism and working equipment (unlike the previous drummer's broken hi-hats) immediately impressed the band. He initially recorded a 5-song EP with them, some of which was done in his basement facilities. "Then when we met Tim, it was like, whoa, this guy is really professional because he was a very accomplished drummer, but his equipment also worked."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Hamilton Local Act and Influence
xref.body: The Constantine's were a band that frequently played in Hamilton venues like the Casbah and Underground around 2006, during what was considered the "Golden Age" of indie rock. Their guitar-driven indie rock sound influenced Arkells' early musical direction, particularly on songs like "The Boss Is Coming." "So every week at the club it seemed like at the Casbore, the Underground there was bands like Winner Sleep or Joel Plasket, Constantine, Stars, Sam Roberts, Arcade for all of these bands just coming through Hamilton that we got to go."

xref.title: Initial Hesitation about Joining Arkells
xref.body: Despite his professionalism, Tim Oxford initially had reservations about joining Arkells. After his first tryout, he told his partner, Sarah, that he probably wouldn't go back, but changed his mind quickly when they began recording together shortly after. "If I'm being totally honest, I went home and I remember Sarah being like, hey, my lady saying, hey, how to go? You were trying out with that band or whatever. And I was like, I don't think I probably won't go back initially."

xref.title: Pre-Arkells Project
xref.body: This was a band that some future Arkells members, including Dan Griffith, were involved with before Arkells became a "going concern." It was described as a "half band cover band" (referencing The Band) with a country-styled musical approach. "Surley Young Box, a pre-Archelles band, recorded when they had a reunion show in 2007, but a year after the Archelles started as a going concern."

xref.title: Warped Tour Appearance
xref.body: Anthony Carone played on the Warped Tour with the band Il Scarlett. He returned from the tour directly to jam with Arkells, still dressed in his Warped Tour attire, including a shaved head and bandana, finding it aesthetically surprising that Arkells accepted him. "I went on Wharp tour and in the middle of that Wharp tour. Who were you playing with for a while? Il Scarlett. Oh, cool. I was with them for a couple of years."
